full_judgment: 63. Section 106 of the Evidence Act enacts the second exception to the general rule that the burden of proof is on a party who asserts the affirmative of a fact. Under this rule, the burden of proof lies on the person who wishes to support his case by a particular fact which lies more particularly within his knowledge. The rule is of general application; it holds good whether the proof of the issue involves the proof of an affirmative or of negative, and has been allowed to prevail against presumption of law. The true purpose of this section is discernible from the first illustration that when a person does an act with some intention other than that which the character and circumstances of the act suggest the burden proving that intention is upon him. It is only in cases where the facts proved by the evidence give rise to a reasonable. inference of guilt unless the same is rebutted, that such inference can be negatived by proof of some fact which, in its nature, can only be within the special knowledge of the accused.
